Dermatology · published research

Chemotherapy-induced alopecia

Two small randomized trials studied different uses: hair regrowth after chemotherapy and prevention when PBM is added to scalp cooling. Results do not establish durable regrowth or added prevention benefit, and quality-of-life findings need separate confirmation.

Summary of the Evidence

Five publications are listed in the exact chemotherapy-induced alopecia category: two small randomized trials, one trial protocol, one commentary, and one rat study. The trials ask different questions: regrowth after chemotherapy versus prevention during chemotherapy with scalp cooling. A broader systematic review included 32 participants with chemotherapy-induced alopecia, but the available data were insufficient for a subtype-specific meta-analysis.

Human and clinical evidence

The HAIRLASER trial randomized 32 breast-cancer patients after anthracycline- and taxane-containing chemotherapy to PBM or no intervention. Treatment started on the final chemotherapy day and involved three sessions weekly for 12 weeks. Blinded reviewers reported a higher hair-growth score at one month, but the difference was not maintained at months two and three. Global-health scores were higher in the PBM group at the reported assessment points (Lodewijckx et al. 2023).

A separate 29-person randomized trial added PBM to scalp cooling during chemotherapy. Scalp coverage and hair thickness did not differ significantly between the groups; global-health, physical, role, and social-functioning scores favored the PBM group. These quality-of-life outcomes are separate from the hair-loss prevention result (Claes et al. 2025).

A Taiwanese randomized-trial protocol describes a home-use helmet-type low-level light device for 106 women with breast cancer and chemotherapy-induced alopecia, randomized 53 per group. It plans 12 treatment courses over four weeks; it is a protocol and does not report trial outcomes (Wu et al. 2023).

A systematic review of alopecia subtypes included 32 participants with chemotherapy-induced alopecia among 3,098 participants overall. The authors reported insufficient statistics to pool results for this subtype, so the review does not provide a CIA-specific PBM effect estimate (Perez et al. 2024).

Animal evidence

In a rat model, 655-nm low-level laser treatment accelerated hair regrowth after chemotherapy. The report did not establish clinical benefit or safety in people receiving chemotherapy (Wikramanayake et al. 2013).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

In the HAIRLASER trial, the PBM protocol used 678 nm, 1.03 J/cm² per treatment, and 20 min per session, three times a week for 12 weeks (36 sessions). The prevention trial evaluated PBM only as an addition to scalp cooling, not as stand-alone prevention. These distinct protocols do not establish an optimal schedule.

Interpretation

The post-chemotherapy trial reports a short-term hair-growth signal that was not maintained at later follow-up, while the prevention trial did not show added benefit on scalp coverage or hair thickness. Current human evidence does not establish reliable prevention or durable regrowth. The quality-of-life findings are encouraging but need adequately powered replication.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low for short-term hair regrowth after chemotherapy.

Very low for prevention when PBM is added to scalp cooling.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Two small randomized trials address separate uses. One reports a higher hair-growth score at one month after chemotherapy, with no maintained difference at later follow-ups. The scalp-cooling trial found no significant difference in coverage or thickness. Larger trials with consistent schedules, blinded assessment, and follow-up are needed for each question.
